docs.title: Kinetic-Solver
docs.text:
A finite volume solver for the one-dimensional Saint-Venant (shallow water) system with topography, built around the kinetic scheme with reflections of B. Perthame and C. Simeoni (Calcolo, 2001).

\[ \partial_t h + \partial_x (hu) = 0, \qquad \partial_t (hu) + \partial_x\!\left(hu^2 + \tfrac{g}{2}h^2\right) = -g\,h\,\partial_x Z . \]

The scheme treats the bottom \(Z\) as a potential barrier for fictitious particles: particles cross a step when they have enough kinetic energy and are reflected otherwise. This gives a finite volume method that

  • keeps the water height non-negative, dry areas included;
  • preserves the lake at rest (\(u = 0\), \(h + Z\) constant) exactly;
  • satisfies a discrete entropy inequality;
  • stays stable on discontinuous bottoms.

A Rusanov scheme with hydrostatic reconstruction (Audusse et al., 2004) is included for comparison.

docs.title: In thirty seconds
docs.text:
make
./build/kinetic-solver --case dam-break-wet --cells 400 --snapshot-every 20
python3 scripts/plot.py output --animate
make test

docs.title: Status
docs.text: The scheme of the paper is implemented and checked against its definitions to round-off (see Validation). The code was first written in 2013; the 2026 revision fixed several bugs (including a truncated value of π that broke the lake-at-rest property), restructured the code and added a test suite. The original guide, Guidebook.pdf in the repository, describes the 2013 version.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
make test     # needs python3 with numpy and scipy
File What it checks tests/test_fluxes.py kinetic fluxes against the definitions of the paper; mass flux single-valued; momentum interface law of Ersoy (2026); hydrostatic balance; Rusanov on flat bottoms and dry states; Stoker's middle state tests/test_solver.py lake at rest on three topographies; errors against Ritter and Stoker; convergence; positivity; mass conservation; command line tests/test_cases.py the exact solutions themselves (Bernoulli head, critical crest, jump position, periodicity of Thacker's solution); Thacker's bowl; the three steady flows over the bump; run-up and backwash on the beach tests/test_integrators.py order in time of each integrator; SSP properties; Euler versus Runge-Kutta; mirror and translation symmetries; options

tests/flux_harness.c exposes single interface fluxes to the Python tests: it reads scheme hL huL zL hR huR zR lines and prints the two fluxes.

GitHub Actions builds the code with gcc and clang (warnings are errors) and runs the tests on every push and pull request.

Before submitting a change to the numerics, it is worth also running the suite under the sanitizers:

make clean
make CFLAGS="-std=c99 -O1 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -Wall -Wextra"
make test CFLAGS="-std=c99 -O1 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -Wall -Wextra"

docs.title: Adding a scheme
docs.text:
A scheme is a pair of functions and an entry in the table of src/scheme.c:

/* Fluxes at the interface between `left` and `right`, seen by each cell. */
void my_interface_flux(CellState left, CellState right, Flux *seen_by_left, Flux *seen_by_right);

/* Bound on the particle or wave speeds, for the CFL condition. */
double my_wave_speed(double h, double hu);

static const Scheme schemes[] = {
    ...
    {"my-scheme", "one-line description", my_interface_flux, my_wave_speed, 0.9},
};

The two fluxes differ only when the scheme accounts for the bottom at the interface; on a flat bottom they must be equal. Add the new scheme to the SCHEMES tuples of the tests: the lake-at-rest, conservation and symmetry tests then cover it.

docs.title: Adding a test case
docs.text: A case is an entry in the table of src/cases.c: domain, final time, default number of cells, boundary condition, the primitive of the bottom (cell averages are computed from it), the initial condition and, if one is known, the exact solution. The primitive receives the case, so the topography can depend on its parameters. If the domain is symmetric about \(x = 0\), the case can also take part in the mirror test. An exact solution is worth checking on its own before comparing a scheme with it: tests/test_cases.py does so for the solutions added in 2026, and caught a wrong jump position that way.

docs.title: Adding a time integrator
docs.text: An integrator is a list of Shu-Osher stages \((a_k, b_k)\) in src/integrator.c. Keep \(a_k, b_k \ge 0\) and \(a_k + b_k = 1\) so that it stays strong-stability-preserving, and add it to INTEGRATORS in tests/test_integrators.py with its expected order.

docs.title: Updating the documentation
docs.text:
The documentation lives in docs/ and is built with MkDocs Material:

pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve            # http://127.0.0.1:8000, reloads on change
mkdocs build --strict   # what the CI runs

The pages also render directly on GitHub. Figures and tables of the Validation page come from

make && python3 scripts/make_doc_figures.py

which writes the PNG files to docs/assets/ and prints the tables.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• C99, no dependency beyond libm; -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow clean.
  • Double precision everywhere; physical constants in src/physics.h.
  • Bottom jumps are seen from the cell that owns the flux (see Implementation).
  • A numerical change comes with a test that fails without it.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
The solver is plain C99 and only needs a C compiler and libm.

make            # builds build/kinetic-solver
make clean

The tests and plotting scripts need Python 3 with numpy, scipy and matplotlib.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
./build/kinetic-solver --list          # cases, schemes and integrators
./build/kinetic-solver --case dam-break-dry --scheme kinetic --cells 400
Option Meaning Default --case NAME test case (see below) lake-at-rest --scheme NAME kinetic or rusanov kinetic --integrator NAME euler, ssp-rk2 or ssp-rk3 euler --cells N number of cells per case (1000) --t-end T final time in seconds per case --cfl C CFL number 0.95 (kinetic), 0.9 (Rusanov) --dt DT constant time step instead of the CFL one — --output-dir DIR where the files go output --snapshot-every K also write a snapshot every K steps initial and final only --no-snapshots only write summary.json — --mirror start from the mirror image \(x \to -x\) of the case — --shift-cells K periodic cases: start from the case shifted by K cells — --verbose print every time step —

--mirror and --shift-cells exist for the symmetry tests. With --dt, steps where the time step exceeded the CFL limit are counted in summary.json; a run whose solution stops being finite stops with an error.

docs.title: Test cases
docs.text:
Case Bottom Initial state Boundaries Exact solution lake-at-rest parabolic bump \(h + Z = 2\), \(u = 0\) free steady lake-at-rest-step step of 0.3 m \(h + Z = 1\), \(u = 0\) free steady lake-at-rest-island bump \(h + Z = 0.1\): the top is dry free steady dam-break-dry flat \(h = 1 \mid 0\) free Ritter dam-break-wet flat \(h = 2 \mid 1\) free Stoker dam-break-bump bump \(h = 2 \mid 1\) free — periodic-pulse flat moving Gaussian pulse periodic — sloshing bump \(h = 2 \mid 1\) walls — thacker parabolic bowl tilted plane surface at rest, both shorelines move walls Thacker bump-subcritical bump lake at rest, then inflow \(q = 4.42\) inflow / outflow steady, Bernoulli bump-transcritical bump lake at rest, then inflow \(q = 1.53\) inflow / outflow steady, Bernoulli bump-hydraulic-jump bump lake at rest, then inflow \(q = 0.18\) inflow / outflow steady, with a jump beach-runup flat, then a 10% beach wave travelling towards the dry beach walls —

The domains are \([-10, 10]\) m, except \([-10, 15]\) m for the flows over the bump and the beach. The bump is \(Z(x) = 0.2 - 0.05\,x^2\) on \([-2, 2]\); the bowl is \(Z(x) = 0.5\,(x^2/64 - 1)\); the beach is \(Z(x) = 0.1\,x\) for \(x \ge 0\).

The flows over the bump take 100 to 200 s of simulated time to settle into their steady state; thacker runs for one period of the oscillation (16.05 s). Runs longer than the default only need --t-end.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
Each run writes to --output-dir:

  • summary.json: case, scheme, integrator, number of cells and steps, CFL number, final time, wall time, initial and final mass, minimum water height over the run, CFL violations, and the L1 and maximum errors of \(h\) and \(hu\) when an exact solution exists (null otherwise).
  • snapshot_NNNNN.dat: one line per cell with the columns x z h hu, plus h_exact hu_exact when an exact solution exists. Two header lines start with #.
  • times.dat: index time for every snapshot.

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
python3 scripts/plot.py output             # output/final.png
python3 scripts/plot.py output --all       # one PNG per snapshot
python3 scripts/plot.py output --animate   # output/animation.gif

In MATLAB or GNU Octave, graph('output') animates the same files.

docs.title: Code organisation
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    main["main.c<br/>options, output"] --> sim["simulation.c<br/>owns grid and buffers"]
    sim --> int["integrator.c<br/>Euler, SSP-RK2, SSP-RK3"]
    sim --> cases["cases.c<br/>topography, initial data,<br/>boundaries, exact solutions"]
    int --> scheme["scheme.c<br/>flux balance L(U)"]
    scheme --> kin["kinetic.c<br/>Perthame-Simeoni"]
    scheme --> rus["rusanov.c<br/>hydrostatic reconstruction"]
    kin --> quad["quadrature.c<br/>tanh-sinh"]
    main --> out["output.c<br/>snapshots, errors"]
File Responsibility grid.c uniform grid, cell centres, state arrays \(h\), \(hu\), \(Z\) cases.c test cases: bottom, initial state, boundary conditions, exact solutions scheme.c the spatial operator: one pass over the interfaces, flux balance per cell kinetic.c interface fluxes of the kinetic scheme with reflections rusanov.c interface fluxes of the reference scheme quadrature.c tanh-sinh quadrature for \(II^q_3\) integrator.c explicit time integrators in Shu-Osher form simulation.c one run: creation, time stepping, destruction output.c snapshot files, error norms main.c command-line options, summary

Schemes, integrators and cases are each a table of entries looked up by name, so adding one does not touch the rest of the code (see Contributing).

docs.title: Grid
docs.text:
The domain \([x_{\min}, x_{\max}]\) is divided into \(n\) cells of width \(\Delta x = (x_{\max} - x_{\min})/n\). Interior cells are \(i = 1, \dots, n\), with centres \(x_i = x_{\min} + (i - \tfrac12)\Delta x\); cells \(0\) and \(n + 1\) are ghost cells filled by the boundary conditions.

The bottom is stored as cell averages, \(Z_i = \frac{1}{\Delta x}\int_{C_i} Z(x)\,dx\), as in Section 3.1 of the paper. Each topography is defined by its primitive, so the averages are exact.

docs.title: Sign convention for the bottom jump
docs.text:
The jump is always the one seen from the cell that owns the flux:

\[ \Delta Z_{i+1/2} = Z_{i+1} - Z_i, \qquad \Delta Z_{i-1/2} = Z_{i-1} - Z_i . \]

A positive jump is a step up for particles leaving cell \(i\). This is the convention the proof of the lake-at-rest property uses (\(\Delta Z_{i-1/2} = h_i - h_{i-1}\) at rest).

docs.title: Interface fluxes
docs.text:
Both schemes implement the same interface: given the states of the two cells on each side of an interface, return the flux seen by the left cell (\(F^-\)) and the flux seen by the right cell (\(F^+\)). scheme_flux_balance visits each of the \(n + 1\) interfaces once and forms

\[ D_i = F^-_{i+1/2} - F^+_{i-1/2}, \qquad \frac{dU_i}{dt} = -\frac{D_i}{\Delta x}. \]

For the kinetic scheme, only \(F^-\) is coded. \(F^+\) is obtained by the mirror symmetry \(x \to -x\): the right cell becomes the "own" cell of a mirrored problem in which velocities change sign. The mass flux changes sign under the mirror and the momentum flux (a second moment in \(\xi\)) does not:

\[ F^{+}_{i+1/2}(U_i, U_{i+1}) = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} F^{-}\big(\tilde U_{i+1}, \tilde U_i\big), \qquad \tilde U = (h, -hu, Z). \]

This halves the code and guarantees that left and right fluxes are computed consistently.

docs.title: The integral II<sub>3</sub><sup>q</sup>
docs.text:
\(II^q_3\) has no elementary primitive. When the bottom steps down towards the own cell (\(K^+ < 0\)), the radicand \((\omega + Fr)^2 + K^+\) vanishes exactly at the upper bound \(\beta = -\sqrt{(K^+)_-} - Fr\), and \(s(\omega) = \sqrt{1 - \omega^2}\) vanishes at the lower bound \(-1\). The integrand therefore has square-root singularities at both ends.

The paper suggests a repeated midpoint rule. Because of the singularities it converges only like \(N^{-3/2}\), and since the lake-at-rest property relies on exact integrals, the quadrature error shows up directly as spurious currents:

Quadrature of \(II^q_3\) max \(\lvert hu \rvert\) after 1.5 s on the lake at rest midpoint, \(N = 100\) \(1.8 \times 10^{-3}\) midpoint, \(N = 1000\) \(5.2 \times 10^{-5}\) midpoint, \(N = 10\,000\) \(\approx 2 \times 10^{-6}\) tanh-sinh, 113 nodes \(1.4 \times 10^{-14}\)

The midpoint figures were measured on the 2013 code in double precision with π corrected (1000 cells); the last line is the current code.

The code uses a tanh-sinh (double exponential) rule, which converges exponentially even with algebraic endpoint singularities. The integrand receives the distances to both endpoints, computed without cancellation, and the radicand is expanded around \(\beta\) so that its exact zero is preserved. Against a 30-digit reference the relative error is below \(2 \times 10^{-15}\).

docs.title: A sign in the paper
docs.text: The closed form of \(II^h_3\) printed in the paper ends with \(-\tfrac12 Fr\,\beta\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). Integrating \(\sqrt{1 - \omega^2}\) over \([-1, \beta]\) gives \(+\tfrac12 Fr\,\beta\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\), which is what the code uses and what matches the flux definition (3.5) numerically.

docs.title: Dry cells
docs.text: Cells with \(h \le 10^{-10}\) are treated as dry: zero velocity, zero Froude number, and no contribution to the fluxes. Both schemes keep \(h \ge 0\) under their CFL condition; after each stage the code only removes round-off level negative values and the momentum of cells that just dried out.

docs.title: Time integration
docs.text:
The semi-discrete system \(dU/dt = L(U)\) is advanced by explicit integrators written in Shu-Osher form,

\[ U^{(0)} = U^n, \qquad U^{(k)} = a_k U^n + b_k\left(U^{(k-1)} + \Delta t\, L(U^{(k-1)})\right), \qquad U^{n+1} = U^{(s)}, \] Integrator \((a_k, b_k)\) Order euler \((0, 1)\) 1 ssp-rk2 \((0, 1),\ (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)\) 2 ssp-rk3 \((0, 1),\ (\tfrac34, \tfrac14),\ (\tfrac13, \tfrac23)\) 3

With \(a_k, b_k \ge 0\) and \(a_k + b_k = 1\), every stage is a convex combination of forward Euler steps (strong-stability-preserving methods with coefficient 1). Positivity, the lake at rest and conservation therefore carry over from Euler under the same CFL condition. The time step comes from the CFL condition (3.9) with a default CFL number of 0.95.

Forward Euler is the scheme of the paper and remains the default: with a first-order space discretisation it is also the most accurate at large CFL numbers (see Validation).

docs.title: The Rusanov reference scheme
docs.text:
The reference scheme combines the Rusanov (local Lax-Friedrichs) flux with the hydrostatic reconstruction of Audusse et al. (2004). At each interface the heights are reconstructed above the highest of the two bottoms,

\[ Z^* = \max(Z_i, Z_{i+1}), \qquad h_i^* = (h_i + Z_i - Z^*)_+, \qquad h_{i+1}^* = (h_{i+1} + Z_{i+1} - Z^*)_+, \]

the Rusanov flux \(\mathcal{F}\) is evaluated on the reconstructed states, and each side adds the pressure correction

\[ F^-_{i+1/2} = \mathcal{F} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \tfrac{g}{2}\left(h_i^2 - h_i^{*2}\right) \end{pmatrix}, \qquad F^+_{i+1/2} = \mathcal{F} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \tfrac{g}{2}\left(h_{i+1}^2 - h_{i+1}^{*2}\right) \end{pmatrix}. \]

It is positive and preserves the lake at rest, dry areas included. Its time step uses the wave speed \(\lvert u\rvert + \sqrt{gh}\) with a default CFL number of 0.9.

docs.title: Boundary conditions
docs.text:
Kind Ghost cells Used by free (transmissive) copy of the neighbouring cell lakes at rest, dam breaks wall copy, with \(hu\) reversed sloshing periodic copy of the opposite end periodic-pulse inflow / outflow left: imposed discharge \(q\), height copied; right: imposed height \(h_{\text{out}}\) while the outflow is subcritical, copy once it is supercritical flows over the bump

The outflow condition follows the characteristics: at a subcritical outlet one wave enters the domain and the downstream height must be imposed; at a supercritical outlet none does and imposing it would be wrong. With a plain copy instead, any subcritical steady state is compatible with the boundary and the transcritical flow never develops: water piles up downstream.

The bottom of the ghost cells follows the same rule, so that a lake at rest stays at rest across the boundary.

docs.title: History
docs.text: The 2013 code had the same scheme but several bugs, found and fixed in 2026: a value of π truncated to 3.1415 (it broke the lake-at-rest property by mixing with acos), an error norm multiplied by \(\Delta x\), a Rusanov scheme without topography that produced NaN on dry beds, three different cell-position formulas, and periodic boundaries one step behind. The pull requests on GitHub give the details and the measurements.

The scheme implemented here: kinetic formulation, interface densities with reflections, properties (Theorem 3.2) and closed-form fluxes (Section 4).

docs.title: Theory
docs.text: This page summarises the mathematics the code implements. Equation numbers such as (3.9) refer to Perthame & Simeoni (2001); see References.

docs.title: The Saint-Venant system
docs.text:
With \(h \ge 0\) the water height, \(u\) the velocity, \(q = hu\) the discharge, \(Z(x)\) the bottom and \(g\) the gravity,

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_t h + \partial_x (hu) &= 0, \\ \partial_t (hu) + \partial_x\!\left(hu^2 + \tfrac{g}{2} h^2\right) &= -g\,h\,\partial_x Z . \end{aligned} \]

The system is hyperbolic for \(h > 0\), with wave speeds \(u \pm \sqrt{gh}\); it loses strict hyperbolicity at \(h = 0\) (dry areas). Two properties matter for the numerics:

  • Steady states at rest. Every state with \(u = 0\) and \(h + Z = H\) constant (a lake at rest) is steady: the pressure gradient exactly balances the bottom slope. A scheme that does not reproduce this balance creates spurious currents over any non-flat bottom.
  • Energy. The energy \(E = \tfrac12 h u^2 + \tfrac{g}{2} h^2 + g Z h\) is conserved by smooth solutions and decreases across shocks: \(\partial_t E + \partial_x\!\big(u (E + \tfrac{g}{2} h^2)\big) \le 0\).

docs.title: Kinetic formulation
docs.text:
The kinetic approach describes the water as a density \(f(t, x, \xi)\) of fictitious particles moving at velocity \(\xi\). The macroscopic quantities are its moments, and at equilibrium the density is a Maxwellian

\[ M(h, \xi - u) = \sqrt{h}\;\chi\!\left(\frac{\xi - u}{\sqrt{h}}\right), \qquad \chi(\omega) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\pi \sqrt{g}} \left(1 - \frac{\omega^2}{2g}\right)_+^{1/2}, \]

which satisfies

\[ \int M \, d\xi = h, \qquad \int \xi M \, d\xi = hu, \qquad \int \xi^2 M \, d\xi = hu^2 + \tfrac{g}{2} h^2 . \]

The Saint-Venant system is then equivalent to the single linear transport equation

\[ \partial_t f + \xi\, \partial_x f - g\, \partial_x Z\; \partial_\xi f = Q, \]

where the collision term \(Q\) has zero mass and momentum and relaxes \(f\) towards \(M\). The bottom acts as a force on the particles: along a trajectory their mechanical energy \(\tfrac12 \xi^2 + g Z\) is conserved.

The half-ellipse \(\chi\) is not arbitrary: it is the density that minimises the kinetic energy \(\int \big(\tfrac12 \xi^2 f + \tfrac{\pi^2 g^2}{6} f^3 + g Z f\big)\, d\xi\) under the constraints of given \(h\) and \(hu\) (Lemma 2.3). This choice is what gives the scheme its entropy inequality. Its compact support, \(|\xi - u| \le \sqrt{2gh}\), also bounds the particle speeds, which is where the CFL condition comes from.

docs.title: The scheme with reflections
docs.text:
The domain is divided into cells \(C_i\) of width \(\Delta x\), with piecewise constant bottom \(Z_i\). At each time step the density is reset to the local Maxwellian \(M_i^n\) ("all collisions at once") and transported upwind:

\[ f_i^{n+1}(\xi) = M_i^n(\xi) - \frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x}\,\xi\left(M^-_{i+1/2}(\xi) - M^+_{i-1/2}(\xi)\right). \]

The bottom jump at an interface is treated as a potential barrier. Write \(\Delta Z_{i+1/2} = Z_{i+1} - Z_i\) and \(\Delta Z_{i-1/2} = Z_{i-1} - Z_i\): the jump seen from cell \(i\). Particles leaving cell \(i\) through its right interface with velocity \(\xi > 0\) are counted directly. The particles arriving from the right (\(\xi < 0\)) are of two kinds:

  • particles of cell \(i\) that tried to climb the step without enough energy, and come back reflected with velocity \(-\xi\) (when \(\xi^2 \le 2g\,\Delta Z_{i+1/2}\));
  • particles of cell \(i+1\) that crossed the step, their speed changed by the energy balance \(\tfrac12 \xi^2 = \tfrac12 \xi'^2 + g\,\Delta Z_{i+1/2}\).

This gives, for \(\xi \le 0\),

\[ M_{i+1/2}(\xi) = M_i(-\xi)\,\mathbb{1}_{\xi^2 \le 2g\Delta Z_{i+1/2}} + M_{i+1}\!\left(-\sqrt{\xi^2 - 2g\Delta Z_{i+1/2}}\right)\mathbb{1}_{\xi^2 \ge 2g\Delta Z_{i+1/2}}, \]

and symmetrically at \(x_{i-1/2}\) for \(\xi \ge 0\), with \(M_{i-1}\) and \(+\sqrt{\xi^2 - 2g\Delta Z_{i-1/2}}\). The interface densities are then

\[ M^-_{i+1/2} = M_i\,\mathbb{1}_{\xi \ge 0} + M_{i+1/2}\,\mathbb{1}_{\xi \le 0}, \qquad M^+_{i-1/2} = M_{i-1/2}\,\mathbb{1}_{\xi \ge 0} + M_i\,\mathbb{1}_{\xi \le 0}. \]

Taking moments gives the finite volume scheme

\[ U_i^{n+1} = U_i^n - \frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x}\left(F^-_{i+1/2} - F^+_{i-1/2}\right), \qquad F^\pm = \int \xi \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \xi \end{pmatrix} M^\pm(\xi)\, d\xi . \]

The source term never appears as a volume term: it is entirely carried by the difference between the flux seen from the left of an interface, \(F^-\), and the flux seen from its right, \(F^+\) (interfacial upwind sources).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Under the CFL condition (3.9)

\[ \Delta t \, \max_i \left(|u_i^n| + \sqrt{2 g h_i^n}\right) \le \Delta x, \]

the scheme (Theorem 3.2)

  1. keeps \(h_i^n \ge 0\): \(f_i^{n+1}\) is a convex combination of non-negative densities;
  2. satisfies a discrete in-cell entropy (energy) inequality;
  3. preserves every lake at rest: when \(u_i = 0\) and \(h_i + Z_i\) is constant, \(M^-_{i+1/2} = M^+_{i-1/2} = M_i\), so nothing moves.

The mass flux is single-valued: \(F^{h,-}_{i+1/2} = F^{h,+}_{i+1/2}\) (Remark 3.1), so water is conserved exactly. The momentum fluxes differ across a step, which is how the bottom force enters.

docs.title: Closed-form fluxes
docs.text:
With the dimensionless numbers

\[ Fr_i = \frac{u_i}{\sqrt{2 g h_i}}, \qquad K^-_{i+1/2} = \frac{\Delta Z_{i+1/2}}{h_i}, \qquad K^+_{i+1/2} = \frac{\Delta Z_{i+1/2}}{h_{i+1}}, \]

and \((a)_+ = \max(a, 0)\), \((a)_- = \max(-a, 0)\), the flux seen from cell \(i\) is

\[ \begin{aligned} F^{h,-}_{i+1/2} &= \frac{2\sqrt{2g}}{\pi}\left[h_i^{3/2}\left(II^h_1 + II^h_2\right) + h_{i+1}^{3/2}\, II^h_3\right], \\ F^{q,-}_{i+1/2} &= \frac{4g}{\pi}\left[h_i^{2}\left(II^q_1 + II^q_2\right) + h_{i+1}^{2}\, II^q_3\right], \end{aligned} \]

where, writing \(s(\omega) = (1 - \omega^2)_+^{1/2}\),

Integral Particles Definition \(II^h_1\), \(II^q_1\) of cell \(i\), leaving to the right \(\int_{\omega \ge -Fr_i} (\omega + Fr_i)^{k}\, s(\omega)\, d\omega\) \(II^h_2\), \(II^q_2\) of cell \(i\), reflected by an upward step \(\mp\int_{-Fr_i}^{\sqrt{(K^-)_+} - Fr_i} (\omega + Fr_i)^{k}\, s(\omega)\, d\omega\) \(II^h_3\) of cell \(i+1\), crossing to the left \(\int_{\omega \le -\sqrt{(K^+)_-} - Fr_{i+1}} (\omega + Fr_{i+1})\, s(\omega)\, d\omega\) \(II^q_3\) of cell \(i+1\), crossing to the left \(-\int_{\omega \le -\sqrt{(K^+)_-} - Fr_{i+1}} (\omega + Fr_{i+1})\sqrt{(\omega + Fr_{i+1})^2 + K^+}\; s(\omega)\, d\omega\)

with \(k = 1\) for the mass (\(h\)) and \(k = 2\) for the momentum (\(q\)); the sign of \(II_2\) is \(-\) for the mass and \(+\) for the momentum. All of them have elementary primitives except \(II^q_3\) (Remark 4.1), which must be computed numerically (see Implementation). The flux seen from the right, \(F^+\), follows from the same formulas by the symmetry \(x \to -x\).

docs.title: The momentum interface law (Ersoy, 2026)
docs.text:
M. Ersoy revisited the scheme in a discontinuous Galerkin setting and identified the macroscopic law it selects at a bottom jump. The defect between the two one-sided momentum fluxes is exactly

\[ F^{q,-}_{i+1/2} - F^{q,+}_{i+1/2} = g\,\Delta Z_{i+1/2}\; h^{\text{jump}}_{i+1/2}, \qquad h^{\text{jump}}_{i+1/2} \ge 0, \]

where \(h^{\text{jump}}\) is an effective interface height built from three groups of particles. With \(\alpha = \sqrt{2g\lvert\Delta Z\rvert}\), \(M^-\) the Maxwellian of the left cell and \(M^+\) that of the right cell, for an upward step (\(\Delta Z > 0\)):

\[ h^{\text{jump}} = \frac{2}{g\Delta Z}\int_0^\alpha \xi^2 M^-(\xi)\,d\xi + 2\int_\alpha^\infty \frac{\xi\, M^-(\xi)}{\xi + \sqrt{\xi^2 - \alpha^2}}\,d\xi + 2\int_0^\infty \frac{\xi\, M^+(-\xi)}{\sqrt{\xi^2 + \alpha^2} + \xi}\,d\xi : \]

reflected particles, particles climbing the step, and particles coming down it. The downward case swaps the roles of the two cells. At rest, \(h^{\text{jump}}\) reduces to the mean height \((h_i + h_{i+1})/2\), which is the hydrostatic pressure jump. For polynomial degree 0 the discontinuous Galerkin scheme of that paper is exactly the finite volume scheme above. The test suite checks this identity numerically.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Every number on this page can be regenerated with

make && python3 scripts/make_doc_figures.py

and most of them are enforced by the test suite (make test).

docs.title: The fluxes against the paper's definitions
docs.text:
The strongest check does not use the code's formulas at all. A Python reference builds the interface densities (3.7)-(3.8) directly from the Maxwellian \(\chi\), integrates their moments in \(\xi\) with an adaptive quadrature, and compares them with the fluxes returned by the C code on random pairs of states: dry cells, supercritical flows and steps in both directions.

Check Agreement kinetic fluxes \(F^-\) and \(F^+\) against (3.5)-(3.8) \(< 10^{-10}\) (relative) mass flux single-valued (Remark 3.1) \(< 10^{-13}\) momentum defect \(= g\,\Delta Z\, h^{\text{jump}}\) (Ersoy 2026, Prop. 4.1) \(3 \times 10^{-14}\) \(II^q_3\) against a 30-digit reference \(< 2 \times 10^{-15}\) (relative)

docs.title: Lake at rest
docs.text:
Maximum deviation from the initial state after 1.5 s, 1000 cells, forward Euler:

Case Scheme max \(\lvert h - h_0 \rvert\) max \(\lvert hu \rvert\) bump, \(H = 2\) kinetic \(3.1 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.4 \times 10^{-14}\) Rusanov \(1.1 \times 10^{-15}\) \(5.6 \times 10^{-15}\) step, \(H = 1\) kinetic \(2.2 \times 10^{-16}\) \(7.6 \times 10^{-16}\) Rusanov \(1.1 \times 10^{-16}\) \(5.1 \times 10^{-16}\) emerged bump, \(H = 0.1\) kinetic \(9.8 \times 10^{-17}\) \(3.8 \times 10^{-17}\) Rusanov \(2.1 \times 10^{-17}\) \(1.3 \times 10^{-17}\)

Both schemes keep the lake at rest to round-off, including the case where the top of the bump is dry. The tests require \(10^{-12}\) for all three integrators.

docs.title: Dam breaks against exact solutions
docs.text:
Dry bed (Ritter). The kinetic scheme follows the dry front better than Rusanov, whose front lags behind the exact one:

Wet bed (Stoker). The rarefaction, the middle state and the shock are captured by both schemes:

Over the bump, with no exact solution: the flow over the obstacle and the waves it reflects.

docs.title: Moving shorelines: Thacker's bowl
docs.text:
In a parabolic bowl the free surface stays a plane that rocks back and forth, with a velocity uniform over the wet region (Thacker, 1981). Both shorelines move up and down the dry slopes, which makes it one of the hardest tests for wet/dry fronts.

L1 error of \(h\) after one period (16.05 s):

Scheme 100 200 400 800 1600 kinetic 0.298 0.171 0.0945 0.0512 0.0272 Rusanov 0.0476 0.0233 0.0134 0.00743 0.00396

Both schemes converge (order about 0.9) and keep \(h \ge 0\) and the mass to round-off. The kinetic scheme has a larger error constant, and the reason is instructive. Fitting the free surface on 400 cells:

tilt at \(T/2\) \(u\) at \(T/2\) tilt at \(T\) \(u\) at \(T\) exact +0.02395 0 −0.02395 0 kinetic +0.02319 +0.0001 −0.02272 −0.0006 Rusanov +0.02370 +0.0086 −0.02375 −0.0146

The kinetic scheme gets the phase right but damps the amplitude by about 5% per period; Rusanov keeps the amplitude but drifts in phase. The damping does not depend on the time integrator or the CFL number, so it is the numerical dissipation of the kinetic fluxes over a smooth slope, consistent with its discrete entropy inequality.

docs.title: Steady flows over a bump
docs.text:
Water enters on the left with a fixed discharge \(q\) and settles into a steady flow over the bump (Goutal & Maurel, 1997; SWASHES, 2013). Along each smooth part of the flow the discharge is uniform and the Bernoulli head \(q^2/(2gh^2) + h + Z\) is constant. Three regimes:

  • subcritical (\(q = 4.42\), outlet height 2): the surface dips over the bump;
  • transcritical (\(q = 1.53\)): the flow accelerates over the bump, becomes critical at the crest and supercritical downstream;
  • with a hydraulic jump (\(q = 0.18\), outlet height 0.33): supercritical after the crest, then a stationary jump back to the subcritical outlet height, located by the Rankine-Hugoniot condition (x = 1.666).

After 100 to 200 s of simulated time, 400 cells:

Case Scheme L1 error of \(h\) max deviation of the discharge subcritical kinetic 0.039 0.10% Rusanov 0.067 0.62% transcritical kinetic 0.048 0.23% Rusanov 0.305 1.6% hydraulic jump kinetic 0.016 20% (in the jump cell) Rusanov 0.066 25% (in the jump cell)

The kinetic scheme is the more accurate of the two on all three regimes. Its discharge stays almost uniform across the bump, where Rusanov's varies by up to 1.6%, and on the transcritical flow Rusanov's upstream level is visibly too low. Both place the jump within two cells of its exact position, and the numerical jump converges to it as the mesh is refined.

The outlet boundary condition matters here: the downstream height is imposed only while the outflow is subcritical (see Implementation).

docs.title: Run-up on a beach
docs.text:
A wave travelling to the right steepens into a bore, runs up a dry beach of slope 0.1, and flows back down. There is no exact solution.

Maximum run-up above still water, and lowest shoreline position during the backwash (initial shoreline at x = 5):

Cells kinetic run-up Rusanov run-up kinetic backwash Rusanov backwash 250 0.255 m 0.285 m x = 4.15 x = 7.75 500 0.348 m 0.363 m x = 4.08 x = 5.48 1000 0.421 m 0.429 m x = 4.04 x = 4.39 2000 0.478 m 0.481 m x = 4.04 x = 4.19

The maximum run-up converges slowly with resolution, as usual for the thin tongue of water at the tip, and the two schemes agree increasingly well. The backwash shows a clear difference: the kinetic scheme drains the beach and pulls the shoreline below its initial position at every resolution, while Rusanov leaves water hanging on the slope on coarse meshes (the shoreline stays at x = 7.75 with 250 cells). This matches a known limitation of the hydrostatic reconstruction (Delestre et al., 2012): when the bottom step between two cells, slope × Δx, is comparable to the water height, it underestimates the velocity and overestimates the height of thin flows, and the error vanishes as the mesh is refined. The kinetic scheme treats the step as a potential barrier instead and drains the beach correctly in this test.

docs.title: Convergence in space
docs.text:
L1 error of \(h\) at \(t = 1.5\) s as the grid is refined (forward Euler, default CFL):

Case Scheme 100 200 400 800 1600 Order dry bed kinetic 0.184 0.117 0.0723 0.0434 0.0255 0.76 dry bed Rusanov 0.370 0.235 0.144 0.0859 0.0502 0.77 wet bed kinetic 0.356 0.210 0.123 0.0703 0.0400 0.81 wet bed Rusanov 0.361 0.221 0.133 0.0786 0.0458 0.78

The schemes are first order; on solutions with a shock or a dry front the observed order is below 1, as expected. The kinetic scheme is about twice as accurate as Rusanov on the dry dam break.

docs.title: Convergence in time
docs.text:
The space discretisation is first order, so on a refined grid the global error is \(O(\Delta x)\) whatever the integrator. The order in time is measured on a fixed grid (100 cells, periodic pulse, \(t = 0.5\) s) against a reference computed with SSP-RK3 and a time step 16 times smaller than the smallest one below:

Integrator \(\Delta t = 0.5/20\) \(0.5/40\) \(0.5/80\) \(0.5/160\) Order Euler \(8.3 \times 10^{-3}\) \(3.8 \times 10^{-3}\) \(1.8 \times 10^{-3}\) \(8.9 \times 10^{-4}\) 1.03 SSP-RK2 \(3.5 \times 10^{-4}\) \(8.6 \times 10^{-5}\) \(2.1 \times 10^{-5}\) \(5.3 \times 10^{-6}\) 2.01 SSP-RK3 \(1.9 \times 10^{-5}\) \(2.3 \times 10^{-6}\) \(2.8 \times 10^{-7}\) \(3.5 \times 10^{-8}\) 3.00

docs.title: Forward Euler versus Runge-Kutta
docs.text:
At the default CFL number, forward Euler is more accurate than SSP-RK2 and SSP-RK3 on the dam breaks. This is not a bug: with upwind fluxes, the time error of forward Euler partly cancels the numerical diffusion of the space discretisation (for linear advection, upwind with Euler at CFL 1 is exact). The Runge-Kutta methods remove this cancellation and reach the error of the semi-discrete scheme at any CFL number; Euler converges to the same value as the CFL number decreases.

Wet dam break, 400 cells, L1 error of \(h\):

Integrator CFL 0.95 0.5 0.25 0.1 0.05 0.02 Euler 0.123 0.170 0.195 0.209 0.214 0.217 SSP-RK2 0.219 0.219 0.219 0.219 0.219 0.219 SSP-RK3 0.219 0.219 0.219 0.219 0.219 0.219

Higher-order time integration pays off together with a higher-order space discretisation (MUSCL reconstruction, or the discontinuous Galerkin extension of Ersoy, 2026).

docs.title: Conservation and positivity
docs.text:
• Mass is conserved to round-off (\(< 10^{-12}\) relative) with periodic boundaries, walls (including Thacker's bowl and the beach), and on the dam breaks before the waves reach the boundaries.
  • The water height never becomes negative, for both schemes and all integrators, including dry fronts.

docs.title: Symmetries
docs.text:
Two metamorphic tests check whole simulations rather than single fluxes:

  • Mirror. Running the mirror image (\(x \to -x\), \(u \to -u\)) of a case gives the mirror image of the solution: dam breaks, an emerged bump and a closed tank, for both schemes and several integrators.
  • Translation. With periodic boundaries, shifting the initial state by \(k\) cells shifts the solution by \(k\) cells.

Both hold to the last bit on x86-64. They catch sign and index errors that no exact solution would reveal: an asymmetric wall boundary condition, introduced on purpose, fails eight of these checks.
